summary: This work models flux line memory in superconducting qubit control as a stateful classical actuator coupled to the quantum system, deriving first-order error generators for each actuator state component using Dyson expansion. Robust CZ pulses are designed by suppressing these generators and minimizing residual flux line state at gate exit, achieving $F_\mathrm{avg}=99.998\%$ for single gates and $99.97\%$ over ten consecutive gates with $2.3\times10^3$ reduction in sequence infidelity versus baseline.
motivation: Flux-tuned CZ gates in superconducting processors suffer from distortions in the control line that persists between gates; conventional predistortion assumes zero initial flux line state but fails when nonzero memory remains from prior gates, causing rapid fidelity degradation in repeated sequences.
method: The flux line dynamics are modeled in state space and coupled to the QCQ Hamiltonian. First-order perturbation theory connects initial actuator state variations to quantum error generators via the free response of the actuator. Two boundary conditions are imposed: memory robustness suppresses first-order errors from inherited actuator state via vanishing logical and leakage generator components, while state closing constrains the residual actuator state written at gate exit to near zero.
result: In a one-pole model, the robust pulse shows a clear first-order plateau up to $x_c\approx3.5\times10^{-3}\Phi_0$ then quartic error growth versus quadratic for baseline. In a three-pole model fitted to measured line response, a 50 ns pulse simultaneously suppresses all three modal error generators and achieves $99.97\%$ fidelity over ten consecutive gates without extra reset time, compared to $20.3\%$ for baseline under identical reuse conditions.
